	“Fashion and entertainment have been overlapping for so long, it only makes sense that we start to interconnect and join each other’s worlds,” Willy Chavarria tells Variety.

	The Mexican American designer puts that philosophy into practice with “El Puente Eterno,” Tequila Don Julio’s new Día de Muertos campaign. Chavarria stepped behind the camera to direct a short film for the spot, inspired by the symbolic pathway of cempasúchil flowers believed to guide loved ones home during the holiday.


	The film centers on Don Julio’s latest 70 Añejo Cristalino Artist Edition bottle, designed by Mexican designer Patricio Campillo, and brings together a largely Mexican and Mexican American creative team. The bottle will make its public debut Sept. 13 during Campillo’s Spring 2027 New York Fashion Week show.

	For Chavarria, who previously designed two Artist Edition bottles for Don Julio, the project marks another step toward expanding his namesake label beyond clothing. “I think of us evolving into a full creative studio,” he says. “We do partnerships, we do cinematic content, we’ve done music collaborations.” Fashion, he adds, will remain “a huge core part of the brand identity,” even as its boundaries continue to stretch.

	That expansion is especially visible this Fashion Week. Chavarria is coming off the launch of his first UGG collaboration, accompanied by the starry “UGG & KISSES” campaign featuring Becky G, Eva Longoria, Danny Trejo and Ivan Cornejo, and was recently nominated for the CFDA’s American Menswear Designer of the Year award. “I’m so grateful. I cannot tell you,” he says of the prestigious nomination. “All of us in this industry are working so hard, and it feels ruthless sometimes.”


	For Chavarria, the increasing crossover between industries is one of fashion’s more promising evolutions. “It’s one of those aspects of how fashion is changing that’s very exciting,” he says.

	Below, Chavarria talks to Variety about his new Don Julio campaign, championing Campillo , his ambitions in filmmaking — and why Pamela Anderson is next on his dream-dressing list.
	
		You’ve worked with Don Julio on the Artist Edition bottles before, but this is a pretty significant expansion of your role. What made you want to move from designing an object to directing the entire world around the brand?	

	It was a slower progression because Don Julio and I have been working together for so long. They’ve been really involved in all of our celebratory events and runway shows and key cultural events with our brand. So it was a very natural evolution to take it to the next level.

	This time we thought it would be really amazing for us to not just celebrate Willy Chavarria, but to bring in another Mexican creative and highlight a new, up-and-coming fashion brand and give Campillo exposure, while I could really be on the back end in the creative process and create the Don Julio world through a new lens. It was really fun. We all had a great time on this campaign.
	
		How did Campillo get involved, and what did he bring to the project that you couldn’t have achieved alone?	

	I’ve been a fan of his for a while, and we became friends both when he started showing in New York and when I started spending more time in Mexico. So I’ve really been a champion for him.

	I thought it would be amazing for Don Julio and me to partner on this and bring him into the bottle design and let him tell the story of Día de los Muertos, which is so incredibly tied to Don Julio and this tequila and this season, from the perspective of another Mexican designer. We actually had photos of his family in the ofrenda in the campaign, so it was really a nice personal thing for him. He really brought the story to life of what Día de los Muertos is: honoring the past and doing it with joy. He was so perfect to articulate that.
	
		Día de los Muertos is so visually recognizable that some parts of it can be cliché. Are there certain images or tropes you consciously wanted to avoid?	

	That is a great question because we were very conscious of that. Our first thought was that we really wanted to highlight the modern, cool aspects of Don Julio and not be cliché, and not deliver what is already top of mind when people think of Día de los Muertos.


	We wanted to be cool and minimal and chic and still celebratory. So we worked through that together as we were developing the concept and the storyboards and the visuals, and everyone involved was very much on the same page with delivering something new.

	It was really fun because everybody — all of the talent that worked on this campaign, for the most part, especially on set — was Mexican. So we had Enrique doing the photography, Carlos Jaramillo doing the direction, the set designer was Mexican. Everybody knew that we wanted to take a new perspective, and it was very instinctive creatively how to avoid the more traditional, cliché aspects of the holiday.
	
		Earlier this year, you talked about wanting to merge music and fashion more aggressively, and you debuted your short film “Eterno.” Is filmmaking becoming a permanent part of the company rather than something you just do around collections?	

	Yeah, I love it. I love any creative process. But what’s so rewarding about cinema and music is you really tap into more people than you do with simply a product. So even though with Don Julio, we’re actually selling the luxury tequila itself, we’re really sharing the story of Don Julio and the story of Día de los Muertos and the joy that exists within that holiday and celebration. So it’s touching everybody who sees it, not just the end consumer.
	
		As a cinema fan, is there any specific filmmaker who inspires you that you’d love to work with at some point?	

	Oh my God. I’ve got so many, but Wong Kar-wai is one of my top.
	
		Do you still think of fashion as the center of what you do, or is Willy Chavarria becoming something closer to a full creative studio in terms of the brand? Where do you see it going?	

	I think of us evolving into a full creative studio, which, in many ways, we are. We do partnerships, we do cinematic content, we’ve done music collaborations. So I absolutely see that part of the business growing.

	But I do believe that the visual foundation of the business will always exist in fashion. What percentage of the business fashion is might vary over time, but fashion will always be a huge core part of the brand identity.
	
		It seems like a lot of brands are interested in merging these different industries right now.	

	I agree. It makes sense because they’ve been overlapping for so long that it only makes sense that we start to interconnect and join each other’s worlds and have more impact and do more creative things. I love it. It’s one of those aspects of how fashion is changing that’s very exciting.

	
		Going into Fashion Week, you were nominated for the CFDA American Menswear Designer of the Year. What did that moment mean for you?	

	Oh gosh, it means so much to me and my team because it’s encouragement. We’re all working so hard. All of us in this industry are working so hard, and it feels ruthless sometimes. But the CFDA Award is one of those things that makes us stop and pause and appreciate. Just the nomination — being next to Ralph Lauren and Todd Snyder and Thom Browne — it’s such a great honor. It really is, just to be in that sentence.
	
		What shows are you looking forward to this fashion week?	

	I’m excited for Zaldy. I love Zaldy. I think he’s really, really genius. He’s done so much costume, and he does Cirque du Soleil. He’s really amazing. He’s showing menswear. You should check it out. It’s his second show.

	And Diotima — I always like to see what she’s doing. Her work is so soulful, and she’s such a wonderful person. You really just feel it in her work. So that one is always a favorite of mine too.
	
		Who do you think is the best-dressed celebrity?	

	That’s a tough one. Who do you think is the best dressed?
	
		I think Colman Domingo is amazing. He always looks really great. He always just comes to mind for some reason. And then, obviously, Zendaya. Maybe my answers are just not that—	

	Those are obvious.
	
		I know those are obvious. I’m trying to think..	

	Also, Zendaya could wear, like, a dirty [trash bag] and still look amazing..
	
		She could but she doesn’t, which I actually kind of respect.	

	Yeah. She turns it out, and she does it really, really well. And props to Law Roach there. You’ve got to give him props.

	I really, really like when people look like they don’t put a lot of effort into what they’re wearing and just have great style. I love that. I love when people look a little disheveled. When people are too done up for the red carpet, I don’t really get a lot out of it.

	I mean, okay: Pam Anderson. Incredible. Incredible. Monumental. I think she’s terrific.
	
		Is there a celebrity you dream of working with at some point that you haven’t yet?	

	Pam Anderson. Chloë Sevigny. Oddly, Jake Gyllenhaal. I think it’s just because I really like his acting, and I’ve followed him over the years. I think he’s really great. I don’t know — who haven’t I already dressed?

title: Variety and Chanel’s Women in Film Dinner: Ayo Edebiri, Lily-Rose Depp, Michelle Yeoh, Courteney Cox and More Light Up TIFF

body:
Variety and Chanel‘s annual Women in Film dinner was the place to see and be chic at the Toronto Film Festival on Friday night.

	The hottest invite of the festival gathered prominent women and nonbinary filmmakers, where the legendary fashion house co-hosted an evening to remember with Variety co-presidents Ramin Setoodeh (also co-editor-in-chief) and Dea Lawrence. 

	When Oscar winner Michelle Yeoh entered the bar for the evening cocktail hour, Emmy winners Sarah Paulson and Colman Domingo greeted her with hugs. Soon, Patricia Arquette breezed in, pulling in her fellow Oscar winner for a quick photo.
	

	That power quartet — plus Chanel ambassadors and actresses Ayo Edebiri and Lily-Rose Depp, Noomi Rapace, Luke Evans, David Harbour, India Amarteifio, Rosalind Eleazar, Cole Sprouse, Amber Midthunder, Jessica Henwick, Charlie Heaton, “I Play Rocky” breakout Anthony Ippolito , Cooper Raiff, Mariana di Girolamo, Emanuela Postacchini, Mackenzie Davis and more — epitomized the top-tier talent who assembled to celebrate the achievements of women and nonbinary filmmakers in this year’s lineup.


	While the term “filmmaker” generally refers to directors, the event saluted many powerful multihyphenates, like actor-director Fala Chen (“Bloodline”) or Courteney Cox, who launched her directorial debut “Evil Genius” out of the fest.

	“At Variety, we’ve made a commitment to cover parity in the entertainment industry and the importance of female representation on the big screen. And while there have been significant strides, there’s still much room for improvement,” said Setoodeh, kicking off the event.
	

	While Hollywood is having a banner year at the movies, Setoodeh noted, none of the top 15 films at the box office were solely directed by women. “That’s why this dinner is so important. It’s an opportunity for you all to network, to come together, to brainstorm,” he said, asking the female filmmakers and producers in the crowd to raise their hands high. “If you’re an executive, here’s who you need to talk to.”

	Lawrence drove that point home, quoting the late Gloria Steinem: “Representation is not just who gets to appear in the story. It’s about who gets to tell the story. And so tonight we celebrate the women who are doing exactly that: creating, directing, writing, producing, and leading the way, opening those doors for the next generation of women.”

	This year’s TIFF lineup proves progress is possible, as 35% of the official selection is directed or co-directed by women, like “Love of Your Life” from Rachel Morrison or “Josephine” by Beth de Araújo. That impressive figure — a goal that TIFF leadership set for 2028, but reached two years early — is made possible when organizations like Chanel and publications like Variety hold Hollywood’s decision-makers to account, said TIFF’s Chief Business and Marketing Officer Jennifer Frees.

	“Chanel and Variety share TIFF’s passion for supporting the remarkable creators who continue to shape the future of culture and of cinema,” Frees said. “So with that in mind, this evening is a celebration of world-class creativity and the community that it fosters.”

	One such initiative is the Chanel Women Creators’ Network, an extension of the TIFF Share Her Journey’s annual Writers’ Lab. “At Chanel, it’s nothing new for us to support women — because our founder was a woman,” said Gregoire Collignon, president of Chanel Canada, referring to Coco Chanel. “Since the ’30s, she was designing and supporting women in film.” This program, established in 2020, continues that legacy, he added, and “reinforces the house’s commitment to championing women in the arts and to creating opportunities for their artistic and personal development.”

	Carol Nguyen is a 2025 fellow whose documentary “Still Night, Burning House” is also debuting at this year’s fest. The 2026 fellows are Shannon Walsh, Hannah Vastinsalo, Shannon Welby and Amelia Eloisa.
	

	“These four exceptional creators represent the vision, the originality and the artistic excellence that define the next generation of filmmaking,” Frees said. “Through their work, they’re expanding perspectives, they’re challenging conventions, and they’re reminding us why diverse stories matter so much.”

	After the speeches, the mingling continued: “Being Heumann” director Sîan Heder and star Ruth Madeley fielded congratulations for how well their film played as the festival’s opening night selection. Next to them, Lauren Miller Rogen (“Babies”) and Seth Rogen chatted with Ziwe Fumudoh. When the party moved upstairs for an intimate, seated dinner, Rogen’s signature laugh rang out above the din of conversation and the clanking of forks and knives. This fashionable crowd was ready to let their hair down and have some fun amid the business of the fest.

title: ‘The Stunt Driver’ Review: Jay Baruchel Takes a Leap into Tepid Biopic Territory
description: In “The Stunt Driver,” Jay Baruchel reteams with his “Goon” director Michael Dowse and takes on a showy lead part as stunt driver Ken Carter, who’s
body:
In “The Stunt Driver,” Jay Baruchel reteams with his “Goon” director Michael Dowse and takes on a showy lead part as stunt driver Ken Carter, who’s best remembered for a jump he didn’t make: a proposed mile-long leap over the St. Lawrence River in a rocket-powered car. The five years spent on that ill-fated project were captured in the 1981 documentary “The Devil At Your Heels,” which “The Stunt Driver” credits as source material but doesn’t improve on. While the technical aspects of the period recreation are impressive, this remake never finds its own reason to exist.
	

	As in the doc, Carter is introduced executing a stunt jump which leaves him injured and begging the crowd not to leave, addressing them from the stretcher before being carried off. That naked lust for the adulation generated by danger is more bluntly stated when Carter repeats variations on “I gotta jump, people like me” as sufficient justification for his extremely dangerous stunt, the requirements of which include constructing a 90-foot ramp to launch the car. The documentary’s archival footage is seamlessly intercut with staged recreations as Carter assembles a small team of enablers: engineer Dick Keller (Ed Helms), sports agent Bill Wilkins (Dan Bakkedahl), goofy Quebecois protege and hype-man Danny Lafortune (Marc Beaupré). In standard biopic fashion, Ken’s wife Gloria (Laurence Lebouef) is relegated to worrying and suffering in the background.


	Granted interviews with surviving friends and access to unused footage from the documentary, Dowse takes particular advantage of a forgotten radio interview in which Carter was hypnotized. While the additional insight from this rediscovered artifact provides the foundation for a degree of vulnerability and self-revelation that the documentary couldn’t tap into, Carter’s fears remains one-note even when grounded in reality. Carter’s naked craving to be liked and the class-based chip on his shoulder take on sinister connotations at moments when Baruchel sounds strangely like Richard Nixon, further muddying the emotional waters.
	

	When not mired in pathos, Baruchel plays Carter as an eccentric showboater, especially in his elaborate dialogue, which is far beyond the quotable but comparatively low-key man shown in the documentary; the final scene’s slow dissolve fade from Baruchel to the real subject only heighten the oddities of the actor’s performance. Speaking to the trade-war tensions of the present moment, “The Stunt Driver” also makes Carter a zealous Canadian patriot who derides rival stuntman Evel Knievel (Ben Foster) as an unwelcome “yankee doodle dandy” and later yells, “I eat Americans like you for breakfast!”

	Besides the additional psychologizing and final 20 minutes, which address Carter’s years after the jump, the film makes one major alteration to the source text. Presumably because the name of the American stunt driver who took Carter’s place on the jump, Kenny Powers (as in the protagonist of “Eastbound & Down”), would be a distraction for many viewers, both name and personality have been changed to Quebecois comic relief Lafontaine. While both the casting and location choices honor Kane and Baruchel’s shared Quebec background, the change of Powers’ nationality omits another logical place to heighten the anti-American angle. (In a very specific feat, the film’s most notable performance is arguably given by Joe Coben as “Devil” director Bob Fortier; the actor’s speech patterns are eerily like the real ‘70s thing to a degree unheard since Jon Voight channeled Howard Cosell in “Ali.”)

	The first 80 minutes toggle between restaging scenes from the documentary while matching its academy ratio, and alternately providing additional context in widescreen, with a third aspect ratio thrown into the mix at the climax. The idea is clear: the documentary shows some but not all of the truth, so the new film is supplemented by a glossier but more emotionally truthful format and complemented at the end by a new format to heighten Carter’s anxiety. DP Sara Mishara does a bravura job of using numerous formats (digital and actual 16mm, as well as 35mm stock, among others) and rendering them period-plausible as well as handsomely lit and colored in their own right. “The Stunt Driver” is, nonetheless, slow going, and less enjoyable than the funnier, springier documentary it takes great pains to expand on.

title: ‘Much Ado About Nothing’ Gets Modern War-Zone Update From Lakeem Rose (EXCLUSIVE)
description: British writer-director Lakeem Rose, is developing his feature debut, a contemporary adaptation of William Shakespeare’s “Much Ado About Nothing,” w
body:
British writer-director Lakeem Rose, is developing his feature debut, a contemporary adaptation of William Shakespeare’s “Much Ado About Nothing,” with Canadian producers Plato Fountidakis and Paul Rapovski and Hong Kong-based producer and casting director Mike Leeder.

	In Rose’s version, the story shifts to a world just after a modern-day war, centering on four returning soldiers who reunite at the house of a family friend. Old grudges resurface alongside fresh romantic entanglements and a scheme that threatens to unravel everyone involved.
	

	The dialogue stays true to Shakespeare’s Early Modern English, paired with subtitles in contemporary English, even as the setting and visual world around the text are reconstructed for today’s viewers. Rose is also folding sequences styled after silent cinema into the modern-day military backdrop.


	“As always, we have to edit these texts to flow as a screenplay. I’ve been studying how filmmakers and performers like Kenneth Branagh and David Harewood bring this language to life,” said Rose. “The language has survived for 400 years for a reason. Our experiment is to change the context around it and see what happens when these characters, relationships and ideas are placed in a world that feels immediate to people now.”

	Fountidakis is producing, with both he and Rapovski steering the project in their roles as managing partners at Fast Motion Films; Clever Creature handles the film’s international sales and distribution. Between them, the two Canadian producers have spent decades working in genre film and television, having contributed to “Enhanced,” “Believer,” “Mutant X,” “Bullet Proof Monk,” “The Chronicles of Riddick,” “Scott Pilgrim vs. the World” and “Lost Girl.” That background in action design and production is expected to inform the look of the film’s military setting, from its locations to its physical action sequences.
	

	“Independent cinema depends on backing new voices with bold tastes,” said Fountidakis. “This modern adaptation has the opportunity to introduce Shakespeare to audiences who might never otherwise engage with his work. Lakeem has a distinctive perspective on the material, and the combination of Shakespearean language, contemporary genre filmmaking and a post-conflict setting gives the project a very fresh identity.”

	Red Packet Media’s Leeder rounds out the producing team. He has been based in Hong Kong since 1990 and has built his career around Asian and international genre titles, having worked on “Rogue One: A Star Wars Story,” Jet Li’s “Fearless,” “Man of Tai Chi,” the “Ip Man” franchise and “The Raid” films.

	“What interests me is the collision of traditions,” said Leeder. “The language remains Shakespeare’s, but the world around it belongs to contemporary genre cinema. Setting ‘Much Ado’ in the aftermath of such immediate conflict gives the romance, humor and deception a new tone, while the silent visual passages allow parts of the story to be told entirely through image. Plato’s genre experience and Lakeem’s background in theatre and music make this a genuinely unusual way into the material.”

	Rose’s path into filmmaking began with an English degree at the University of Oxford, where he appeared in a staging of Shakespeare’s “Love’s Labour’s Lost” under the guidance of Shakespeare scholar Jonathan Bate. His work outside narrative film spans music, visual media and documentary projects.

	A separate documentary series, “Reinventing Shakespeare,” is tracking the film’s progress, following Rose and his collaborators as they work through what Shakespeare’s writing can offer a new generation of viewers.

	Rose and Fountidakis plan to take meetings around the project at the Toronto Film Festival market.

	The adaptation is in development now, with a 2027 release targeted.

title: Ali Asgari Doesn’t Believe in a Bright Future After Iran’s January Massacre – Just ‘A Bit of Light’

body:
Iranian director Ali Asgari has no desire to repeat clichés about great expectations for things to come. 

	“In Iran, we don’t have high hopes for the future anymore,” he states. 

	“We’ve been waiting for good news for so many years, and it never came. But I do believe in these small specks of light. For now, let’s just stick to them so that we can take the next step.”


	Talking to Variety after the premiere of his sixth feature “A Bit of Light,” Asgari – also behind “Disappearance,” “Terrestrial Verses” and “Divine Comedy” – said he wanted to “celebrate simple things.” 
	

	“Right now, especially in my country, we are forgetting about them. We’re forgetting about our families and helping others. We are surrounded by disaster every day, all the time, always expecting something horrible to happen,” he says. 

	“When we wake up, we don’t know if we’ll be able to handle it until nighttime. We’re all living in a dangerous world right now. If after watching this film someone goes to their mother and takes her hand, that’s enough.”

	Family is certainly on the mind of his protagonist, a kind doctor (played by Misagh Zareh) who becomes disillusioned after his arrest. With his medical practice shut down, he’s ready to end his life. He’s a practical man, though, so he decides to tell his family and make suitable arrangements. 

	“Some doctors in Iran were the only witnesses to what was really happening after the massacre in January. They faced so much death and saw so many injured. We couldn’t even talk about it,” he notes.
	

	In January, after weeks of protests, the authorities opened fire on demonstrators.

	“I saw so many families mourning their children. It had affected so many people’s lives. This man still feels connected to his family, and he knows he has to prepare them for what he wants to do. That’s just the way he is.”

	He keeps his pain to himself. 

	“Usually, when we think about sadness or depression, we think of very expressive acting or directing. I took a simpler approach. I told [Misagh]: ‘I only want to see it in your eyes and on your face’.”

	Asgari, who got to show the film in Venice’s main competition, thought a lot about Italian filmmakers. 

	“I studied in Italy, basically. I’ve been inspired a lot by Italian neorealism and people like [screenwriter] Cesare Zavattini. It was important for me to show the everyday life of a country, and I see many similarities between [Iran] and neorealism’s depiction of Italy after the war.” 

	“We are experiencing a horrible tragedy: war and massacres. That’s why it’s so important to focus on normal life.”

	His characters can’t ignore what’s happening entirely – they cook and talk about Trump – but they still need to keep going. 

	“While writing the screenplay, we thought a lot about the absurdity of it all. Albert Camus wrote about Sisyphus rolling a rock to the top of a mountain. Then the rock would roll down, and he had to start over. That’s our life,” says Asgari. 

	“This man decides to act because nothing has changed. In the end, the war still exists, and so does the repression. But then he decides to roll the rock back up the mountain again.” 

	He adds: “That’s also what I’ve learnt from Italian filmmakers like Nanni Moretti. ‘The Son’s Room’ [about parents grieving the death of their son] was a very good example of that.” 

	In the film – sold by Salaud Morisset and produced by Milad Khosravi for Seven Springs Pictures – helping others or simply being with them takes the protagonist’s mind off suicide. 

	“This story is about a man who’s going to take his life, but life follows him everywhere,” says the director. 

	“Our lives are interconnected. Personally, whenever I want to do something, I immediately think of my mother and sisters. How will they react? I know I could destroy their lives, so I’m careful when making decisions,” he says. 
	

	“What we need, especially now, is to be together. Iran is a divided country. I wanted this family to come together, sit side by side and even dance a little. If we want any kind of change, it should happen this way.”

	In Iran, but also in other places.

	“During our premiere, so many people were crying. It didn’t matter where they were from. They just connected with this character, mostly because we’re talking about human values and dignity.”

	“That’s what cinema is for – it can speak your language, and it can speak for everyone. In life, we sometimes hope for big things. But I’m not waiting for a bright future anymore. Just for some light.”

title: Netflix’s ‘Scooby-Doo: Origins’ Wraps Production Ahead of 2027 Release
description: Netflix’s “Scooby-Doo: Origins” has wrapped production, the company announced Sunday. The live-action series is set for a global release on the stre
body:
Netflix’s “Scooby-Doo: Origins” has wrapped production, the company announced Sunday. The live-action series is set for a global release on the streamer in 2027. 

	Per the series’ official logline, “Scooby-Doo: Origins” is a “modern reimagining of the iconic mystery-solving group of teens and their very special dog.”

	“During their final summer at camp, old friends Shaggy and Daphne get embroiled in a haunting mystery surrounding a lonely, lost Great Dane puppy that may have been a witness to a supernatural murder,” the logline continues. “Together with the pragmatic and scientific townie, Velma, and the strange, but ever so handsome new kid, Freddy, they set out to solve the case that is pulling each of them into a creepy nightmare that threatens to expose all of their secrets.” 
	

	The show, which audiences got a first look at earlier this year, was filmed in Atlanta. (Past Netflix productions “Stranger Things” and “His & Hers” were also shot in the state.) 


	The previously announced cast includes McKenna Grace as Daphne Blake, Tanner Hagen as Shaggy Rogers, Abby Ryder Fortson as Velma Dinkley and Maxwell Jenkins as Fred Jones. The titular canine will be played by a real Great Dane — a first for the “Scooby-Doo” universe. 

	The cast also includes Paul Walter Hauser (as Scooby-Doo’s owner), Rusty Schwimmer, Peter Macon, Jona Xiao, Dani Deetté, Elysée Sanvillé, Alex Isles, Avery Kristen Pohl, Pamela Mitchell, Ross Kimball, Sara Gilbert, Wynn Everett, Sauriyan Sapkota, Bruce McGill, André Benjamin and Cathy Moriarty.
	

	Showrunners and writers Josh Appelbaum and Scott Rosenberg (“High Fidelity,” “Everything Sucks!”) executive produce alongside Toby Haynes. Greg Berlanti, Sarah Schechter and Leigh London Redman executive produce via Berlanti Productions and its overall deal with Warner Bros. Television, in addition to André Nemec, Jeff Pinkner and Adrienne Erickson, who executive produce via Midnight Radio. Warner Bros. Television is the studio.

title: Jeremy Thomas Remembered as a Filmmaker ‘Full of Stories’ and a ‘Rebel With Taste’: ‘The Canon of His Work Is Unmatched’
description: Tributes have begun flowing from across the film world for Jeremy Thomas, the legendary British producer who passed away on Friday at the age of 77.
body:
Tributes have begun flowing from across the film world for Jeremy Thomas, the legendary British producer who passed away on Friday at the age of 77.

	Terry Gilliam, who worked with Thomas on “Tideland” and “The Man Who Killed Don Quixote,” told Variety, “Jeremy Thomas loved making movies. He loved every aspect of the business, but most of all he loved directors. The list of those he worked with is almost endless and I was one of the lucky ones. His taste in filmmaking spanned the globe. He was fearless in getting some very unlikely films financed and released, often to worldwide success. The list is remarkable in range and absolutely unforgettable in quality.”
	

	Added Gilliam: “Most of all, he was a joy to work with. As your producer you always felt protected and encouraged, rare qualities to experience, especially when lack of time and money are swirling around you, raging at your head. Filmmaking is not cheap and the pressures are intense but Jeremy always remained calm and supportive. He was a rare and very unique gem in the world of producers.”


	Luca Guadagnino, who recently put Thomas on camera for his Venice-bowing documentary “Joie De Vivre” to talk about Italian director Bernardo Bertolucci (with whom he made five films), offered Variety a heartfelt statement about the producer.

	“Jeremy Thomas’ death leaves a gigantic void. The space he was fulfilling was a space of pure cinema. Someone who knew how to collaborate with filmmakers and make them better, and how to be himself — a great filmmaker,” he said. “The canon of his work is unmatched, and some of the greatest movies of the past 50 years have been produced by him. And the level of the partnerships that he established in his career is incredible, from Nagisa Oshima to Bernardo Bertolucci. He was a generous man. He was a kind man. He was a man full of stories to tell, but at the same time, very curious to hear others people’s stories. I regret not having been able, in my life, to be produced by the great Jeremy Thomas, and I say a very moved goodbye to him.”
	

	Takashi Miike, the Japanese filmmaker who collaborated with Thomas across numerous features, including “Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo,” premiering in Toronto on Monday, sent Variety a message to his dear friend.

	“We promised to celebrate the world premiere here in Toronto and have a good drink together,” he said. “This sudden news came out of nowhere, leaving me completely in shock and deeply saddened. Jeremy gave me my wings — he was a great mentor and an irreplaceable friend. Rest in peace for now. Until we meet again.”

	Mark Cousins, who directed the 2021 documentary “The Storms of Jeremy Thomas,” in which the director travelled by car with Thomas to Cannes, said: “Jeremy conducted an evening, a trip, a holiday like it was an orchestra. Everything flowed. The hotel had the best balcony views. The producer of ‘The Last Emperor’ ordered at a Chinese restaurant and exquisite food arrived. He played music in the car for five days as we drove to Cannes. I felt safe and exalted in Jeremy’s world. Life will never be the same.”

	Thomas was greatly admired and loved by fellow British producers, such as Danny Boyle’s producing partner Andrew Macdonald. Macdonald told Variety that “Jeremy and I bonded over his father [director Ralph Thomas] and my grandfather both producing films for Rank in the 1950s. He was a hero for me. A rebel with taste.” Macdonald’s grandfather was Emeric Pressburger, the co-writer, co-director and producer of “The Red Shoes” and “Black Narcissus,” among other classics.

	Producer Stephen Woolley, whose credits include Oscar-nominated films like “The Crying Game” and “Carol,” told Variety that Thomas was a “colossus.”

	“I first met the maverick and international producer in Tokyo at a buyers’ screening of his movie ‘Merry Christmas Mr. Lawrence.’ Jeremy Thomas was the person in 1981 in Japan who didn’t suggest but insisted that I be a film producer!,” he said. “He was a huge inspiration and a massively undervalued genius and necessary rebel in our industry… he sided with the subversives and movie anarchists and we loved him dearly… and I have to thank him for my career following in similar footsteps avoiding nationalistic stereotypes and embracing the world of cinema.”

	Woolley added that “without Jeremy (and a little help from John Boorman)” he would “never had had the nerve at 27” to make “The Company of Wolves” with Neil Jordan. 
	

	“Jeremy showed with his first movie success ‘The Shout’ (with Polish friend and collaborator Skolimowski) that boundaries were there to be ignored or broken. And that movies are an international and all-embracing experience,” he said.

	“Myself and my producing partner Elizabeth Karlsen look up to his guiding star still moving across the galaxy and inspiring filmmakers from all nations and genders with his extraordinary body of stellar work. Hoping to take guidance from a groundbreaking guru whose love of world cinema defied any easy categorization.”

	Sony Pictures Classics’ Tom Bernard described Thomas as a “very good friend” and also one of the “first people” he met when he started in film distribution.

	“We released ‘The Shout’ together, which was the beginning of a very long friendship and professional relationship. Over the years, we saw each other every year in Cannes and whenever I was in New York, sharing lunches, dinners and, of course, plenty of stories about the movies we loved,” he said. “His accomplishments in cinema were extraordinary, and one of my great regrets is that he was never properly honored by one of the major festivals for his extraordinary contribution to our industry. I’ll always remember being with him at the Oscars when he won Best Picture — he was absolutely thrilled. He was a great friend to Sony Pictures Classics, but, above all, he was a great friend to me. I will miss him tremendously.”

	Producer and publisher Charles Finch said, “He made great movies and was a loyal, dear friend. His father, Ralph, made a film with my father, Peter, called ‘No Love for Johnnie.’ We spent plenty of time talking movies, cars and praising the devilled kidneys as Wilton’s.”

	On social media, Edinburgh Film Festival CEO and director Paul Ridd said that the “loss of Jeremy Thomas is enormous, to film culture and to the world,” adding that he was “such a beautiful man and a extraordinarily generous supporter” of the festival. 

	Adrian Wootton, chief executive of Film London and the British Film Commission, said that Thomas’ passing was, “Such terribly sad news for Jeremy’s loved ones, family, friends, colleagues, the filmmakers and for the British Film Industry he did so much for.”

	Across a career spanning more than half a century, Thomas produced 80 features, championing the work of both international cinema and daring auteur filmmakers in the process. In 1988 he won the best picture Oscar for Bertolucci’s “The Last Emperor.”

title: Melissa Rivers on Her Glorious Return to the Emmys Carpet, Remembering Her Mom Joan and Why ‘It’s Been Really Hard’ to Watch ‘Hacks’
description:
Melissa Rivers is returning to the red carpet.

	Fashion expert and author Rivers — who rose to fame reporting outside awards-shows with her late mo
body:
Melissa Rivers is returning to the red carpet.

	Fashion expert and author Rivers — who rose to fame reporting outside awards-shows with her late mother, the comedian Joan Rivers — will be joining Variety co-president and co-editor-in-chief Ramin Setoodeh and CNN correspondent Elizabeth Wagmeister at the two brands’ Emmys pre-show broadcast. On “CNN & Variety Red Carpet Live: TV’s Biggest Night,” streaming live beginning at 5 p.m. ET on Monday, Sept. 14 at CNN.com/Watch and on the CNN app for CNN’s streaming subscribers, Rivers will provide interviews and commentary. 
	

	Her presence promises to be both a nostalgic look back and a turning of the page, as Rivers insists she wants to strike a tone that’s been absent for a while: As a duo, the Riverses broadcast for E! and for the TV Guide Channel before, in 2007, their association with the red-carpet ended. In 2011, the elder Rivers declared “We’ve done that. It’s not fun anymore.” Melissa agrees, and is hoping to bring a spirit of joie de vivre to the proceedings. The pair continued to host E!’s “Fashion Police,” which Melissa continued after her mother’s 2014 death until the show’s final episode in 2017.


	A few days before her hosting gig, Rivers spoke to Variety about the spirit of “fun” she feels has been missing from the carpet, what she thinks of Jean Smart’s performance as a groundbreaking female comedian and what Joan Rivers would say about celebrity style in the age of Ozempic.
	
		You’re back on the red carpet after a long absence. What does it mean to get to come back?	

	Well, first of all, it’s my first time back in 20 years. It’s crazy. I’m going to give you the timeline: I was originally supposed to join in via Zoom, and do some color — some fun. Then I got a call either Saturday or Sunday [Labor Day] weekend, and they said, “Would you be interested in being on the carpet?” Without really thinking about it, I said “Sure.”
	

	And then 10 minutes later, I was like, “Oh my God!” Suddenly, it dawned on me, I haven’t stood on a red carpet for coverage in 20 years. It became very overwhelming, because I realized I had so much to do.
	
		What does your preparation look like?	

	Luckily, I’ve seen most of the shows. CNN gave me a huge briefing book, and I’m going through the storylines, the actors, the different categories, finding interesting facts. The other day, they’re like, “And here are the presenters!” and I’m like — Oh, God, they have to put more in my brain.

	How I used to do it came back: By storyline, category, and then individuals. Matthew Rhys has won for [“The Americans”], and this is his first time for “Widow’s Bay.” If I end up talking to him, I’m like, “Is there one that you’re more emotionally attached to?” You’ve won, and here you are with your hat in the ring. And with you and Keri Russell — who gets more mirror time?
	
		Right — they’re prepping together.	

	Do you do your fittings at the same time? For my wedding, trying to get my husband, my son, and his two sons coordinated for a fitting, it might as well have been D-Day.

	But I’ve been really outspoken about this: The fun has been gone. The lightness has been gone. It’s not going to be the same as me and my mom; it’s never going to be that again. But there’s a whole new lane for just being fun and lightening up.

	I’m going to be the shallow end of the pool. Don’t come to me if you’re going to want to make statements. I want to know who you’re wearing, and fun stuff. I want to know, was there ever a performance you really thought you were going to get nominated for, and you didn’t?
	
		It felt as if in some point since you and your late mom left the red carpet, the tone of coverage did get more serious. I’m curious what you made of that as an observer.	

	Yeah, it got very, very serious. The one with #MeToo and all the women wore black [the 2018 Golden Globes, at which all female attendees wore black garments in an organized protest], that was great, because there was a theme. Everybody was wearing black, and you got to see actual personalities come through, because of the decisions that the women made. That would have been the greatest “Fashion Police” ever. But that’s really where it turned very serious and statement-oriented.
	

	The world has become so much more serious in the last 20 years. The social reckonings, the political landscape: The world is going to hell in a handbag. But let’s call it what it is. It’s a bunch of beautiful, talented, successful people, walking into a building to see if they won something. The consequence is, Does someone like your dress?
	
		And you’ll be the judge of that!	

	Of course I will. One of the things people used to love was — as my mom used to say, when you sat on your couch at home, you didn’t say everybody looked wonderful. We were just giving voice to that. We tried to be the viewer. That’s why I’m saying: If you want to make a political statement, go to another position. Don’t stop. Because that is not my vibe. Let’s bring fun back.
	
		Are there any attendees whose style you tend to really like?	

	Keri Russell always looks amazing. I’m going through, in my head, who the women are. Jean Smart always looks appropriate and yet glamorous. Who else do we have?
	
		Hannah Einbinder. Zendaya.	

	Oh, forget it. Zendaya — okay, we’re all running for number two. It’s almost like, “Why bother?”
	
		Speaking of Jean Smart, though, I’m curious if her performance on “Hacks” ever called your mom to mind. Many people think Deborah Vance is based in part on Joan Rivers. 	

	Yes, of course. And my mother would be so happy that if there was anyone playing someone lightly based on her, that it was Jean Smart. She would be so happy. Not only is Jean so talented, but she is tall and elegant and blonde. My mother always joked that Cate Blanchett would play her in a movie. She got Jean Smart, which would thrill her to death.
	
		In the fifth season, an Emmy nominee this year, Deborah and her daughter D.J. have a real breakthrough in their relationship. Did you recognize this as true to life, or see yourself in Kaitlin Olson’s performance as D.J.?	

	I actually haven’t watched it yet. 
	
		I’ll sum it up: We leave the relationship in a really positive place overall.	

	It’s really hard for me to watch these things. I can’t speak intelligently about it because I haven’t watched enough of the show for a multitude of reasons. When someone snuck me the pilot, I was not thrilled by how I was portrayed. But I do appreciate that there was an evolution of the relationship. Do I think where my character started was accurate? No. Do I love the fact that they portrayed evolution — which is a true theme between mothers and daughters? I love that.
	
	
		Speaking of mothers and daughters, have you ever re-watched the perennially viral clip of your mom and you walking out of “The Celebrity Apprentice” together after you were fired? 	

	Oh, God, no! I’m not sure if that was one of my greatest moments or one of my worst moments. Hell, no!
	
		I wonder what your mom would have made of the current landscape, where stars are more open about the work they’ve had done and Ozempic has redefined the red carpet.	

	I think she would say, “Thank God — everybody’s caught up! And admitting it!” Back in the day, we would be looking behind people’s ears for fresh scars. Now, everyone’s like, “Look what I’ve done!”
	
		It’s clear you missed the red carpet, even as the prep is a bit stressful. What was it like walking away from awards-show reporting?	

	We chose to walk away because… It’s like anything — you show up and you kind of don’t care. That was when my mom and I had the conversation. We both came to it separately that it was time to walk away.

	I was never planning on this. If you had asked me two weeks ago, “Would I ever go back?,” I would say no. And I still can’t believe I just said “Sure” without really thinking about it. I hate making this more serious than it is — I have a goal, which is to make it fun again. I’m going on my own personal campaign to bring fun back.

title: ‘Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’ Star Adia On Film Debut Opposite Mahershala Ali, Getting Certified as a Doula: ‘Birth Work Fills My Soul’
description: Twenty-five-year-old newcomer Adia never really imagined becoming a movie star. Growing up, she was focused on becoming a professional dancer before
body:
Twenty-five-year-old newcomer Adia never really imagined becoming a movie star. Growing up, she was focused on becoming a professional dancer before a hip injury derailed that dream. That’s when the high school senior discovered acting.

	“I decided to take an acting class, just to try it out and see if that would be comparable or satiate that need to perform and to create,” Adia told Variety via Zoom from her home in Washington, D.C. “I enjoyed it, and I had fun with it, so I just kind of ran with it. I was like, ‘Ok, I’ll go out to L.A.”
	

	Adia has two other major screen credits on her resume — she made her acting debut in the Netflix series “The Midnight Club,” created by Mike Flanagan and Leah Fong, followed by the HBO Max series “Full Circle,” which was directed by Steven Soderbergh. Not a bad start. 


	“Things started to fall in place as soon as I started pursuing acting, and it’s just snowballed,” she said. “It’s just very surreal.”

	Even so, Adia didn’t picture a career making movies — which makes her big screen debut in the action-drama from filmmaker Bassam Tariq (“Mogul Mowgli”) all the more unexpected.

	“Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother,” which debuted on Saturday night at the Toronto International Film Festival, stars two-time Oscar winner Mahershala Ali as Latif, a hired assassin whose secret occupation clashes with his home life when his wife dies suddenly. The film follows Latif as he navigates single fatherhood, including a desperate search for breast milk for his infant daughter. Adia plays Latif’s strong-willed teenage daughter Fatiha, who is forced to grow up quickly as she helps her father care for her younger brother and sister.
	

	“She was just really complex,” Adia said, explaining what drew her to the role. “That’s how young, teenage girls are. But when we see them being portrayed on screen, generally speaking, they are not [complex]. They’re pretty black and white. ‘Oh, she’s just moody, hormonal and thinking about boys, and that’s it.”

	Fatiha was written differently. “This girl has crushes, yeah, but that’s the least of her,” Adia explains. “She is dealing with very deep grief. Then also having to rise to the occasion to be in a maternal role to her siblings. Here is a character with depth, with real emotion. She’s experiencing real-life things in real time and having to navigate them with a 15-year-old brain.”

	“Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” will be released theatrically by Amazon MGM Studios and Orion Pictures. The film debuts in NYC/LA theaters on Sept. 25, followed by a nationwide rollout in October. 

	Adia auditioned for the part over Zoom, then Tariq flew to D.C. to meet her during a 30-minute break she had from her classes. (Adia was studying in a film program with acclaimed Ethiopian filmmaker Haile Gerima.)

	“We didn’t talk too much about the role, but he asked me, ‘How do you envision Fatiha coming to life?’” she recalls. “I did a little bit of research into the name: it’s one of the first openings in the Quran, so it means the opener, the call to action. So we talked a bit about how Fatiha is the call to her father to parenthood, to come forth and be present.” The final step in the process was a chemistry read with Ali.

	“Inside, I was screaming. But I was like, ‘Get the screams out now so that you can be a regular ass bitch on this call, Adia. Like, don’t play around. You’re going to work, so please act accordingly,’” she recalls, laughing.



	

					Adia (as Fatiha), Mahershala Ali (as Latif) and Jahleel Kamara (as Qadir) in “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother,” from Amazon MGM Studios.
									Jaclyn Martinez/Amazon MGM Studios
	



	It was kismet that she and Ali were finally meeting, since she’d auditioned to play his daughter in another project a year prior but didn’t get the part. (“So that was wild, that here I am auditioning again,” she said.) And once she was in the room with Ali, it wasn’t difficult to get in work mode. “Now I’m acting, and it doesn’t really matter who is opposite me; I’m just doing what I love, and hopefully the other person is doing what they love. And thankfully Mahershala loves doing what he does, and so it was magic.”
	

	The role came at the time Adia was undertaking another passion — training for her doula certification.

	“It’s not easy to be a full-time artist. One of the most courageous things that you can do is to commit yourself fully to your artistry,” she said. But there’s a reason behind the “starving artist” stereotype. “You’ve got to support yourself in life,” she continues. “Birth work is something that fills my soul — spiritually and emotionally — but it fills my pockets financially, as well.”

	Her interest in birth work began when she was nine and witnessed her cousin give birth; the experience was life-changing, and she knew she wanted to be a part of that sacred practice as an adult.

	“I was fortunate to be mentored by the midwife and the doula who were at that birth,” Adia said. But her training overlapped with her shooting schedule. “There were days when I would be on my phone in class, and I’d be on set. They’re setting up for a scene, and I have my headphones in one ear, listening to them talking about conception.”

	Adia is now certified — both as a doula and a budding movie star. Her performance in “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” has been hailed as a true standout among a cast that is packed with major talents, including Emmy winner Tramell Tillman, Giancarlo Esposito and John Cho.

	“I do birth work as my day job, and I’ve always thought I’ll probably end up becoming a midwife,” she adds. “Life is constantly shifting and changing. These are my passions: I love film. I love birth work. I’ll see where they meet, or don’t. And what happens next? I don’t know.”

	If and when those movie offers start rolling in, Adia is more prepared than ever after working with Ali. “In my first few projects, I’m new, and I’m thinking, ‘It’s just a blessing to be here. I’m just going to do my job, and I won’t say anything, and I’m not gonna make a ruckus,’” she said. “That’s not a bad thing. That works for some people.”

	But Ali taught her to follow her instincts as an artist and to speak up when she wanted to try something during a take. 

	“Watching Mahershala model that, and then opening the space for me to do that as well, made me feel empowered to be able to show up,” she said. “It was a master class and I got paid for it, which was cool.”

title: TIFF 2026: 20 International Titles to Track, From Feng-I Fiona Roan’s Shuhua Starrer to a Taxidermy Musical and a John Madden Parkinson’s Rom-Com
description: Helen Mirren, Laura Linney, Rhys Ifans, Erin Doherty and James McAvoy star in three of the biggest U.K. titles world premiering at Toronto and makin
body:
Helen Mirren, Laura Linney, Rhys Ifans, Erin Doherty and James McAvoy star in three of the biggest U.K. titles world premiering at Toronto and making Variety’s 2026 selection of 20 International Titles to Track at this year’s Toronto.Jodie Comer sings (very creditably Variety suggests), in a fourth U.K. package, gothic rom-com “Stuffed” as romance takes unpredictable turns at Toronto. 

	As in 2025, multiple more Platform titles, 42% made up of movies from female directors, could have made the selection. It focuses on new titles, hence what otherwise would be startling omissions such as “Jim Queen,” or Spain’s Cannes main competition trio. The list is by no means definitive. But what it does point up is the presence this year of new and noteworthy voices, such as Scotland’s Tom Nicoll and Ireland’s David Turpin. Some of the films may feature in the Oscars race. The Platform selection of Gabriel Martins’ “On Behalf of My Son,” as Variety notes,  consolidates its status as the biggest international hope this year from a Brazilian director.
	

	The selection films will certainly deliver surprises. “Wild Wild East,” for instance, is described as “about many twists and turns, and an ending that throws a straight punch to the head.” 


	And yes, Variety has selected a baker’s score of films. Given the abundance of international movies at Toronto meriting attention, it would prefer to be accused of bad mathematics than bad taste.



	

					Ancestors
									Leanne Sullivan
	



	“Ancestors,” (David Turpin, Samson Films, Lunatica, Ireland, U.K., Discovery)Beau, a young gay man in 1980s London, searches for missing friend Tiny. Featuring Éanna Hardwicke, Jack Wolfe, Jessica Reynolds, Rupert Everett and Christina Hendricks, tenderly scored and shot with many scenes of seeming dreamlike revery, a mystery which soon becomes deeper charting the phantasmagoric emotional landscape and aftermath of the AIDs crisis. “Often when there is an event like this, our instinct is not to look back at it, then sort of not to be aware of the ways in which it’s continuing to haunt us,” Turpin tells Variety. Sold by Mister Smith Entertainment. JH
	



	

					Angh
									Jungle Book Studio
	



	“Angh,” (Theja Rio, Winter Hymns Films, Undercover Squirrel, India, Platform)Theja Rio expands his 2021 short into a feature centered on Anghba, a Nagaland chief presiding over an empty village in the 1960s – his people gone, his wife failing, his son unable to speak. A missionary, played by Douglas Henshall, arrives with gifts and promises that pressure everything Anghba has spent his life protecting. Rio cast the film with Nagaland locals who had never acted before, shooting on 16mm. It’s the London-based writer-director’s feature debut, produced with Nancy Nisa Beso and Bernardo Angeletti, and the only Indian film in this year’s Platform lineup – a section whose winner now heads straight into Oscar’s international feature race. NR



	

					Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo
									Neon
	



	“Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo,” (Miike Takashi, OLM, Nippon TV, Pressman Film, Recorded Picture Company, TF1 Films, U.S., U.K., Japan, France, Special Presentations)Miike Takashi takes the wheel on the third entry in the “Bad Lieutenant” lineage, following Abel Ferrara’s 1992 original and Werner Herzog’s New Orleans reboot, and makes it entirely his own. Shun Oguri plays a gambling-addicted Tokyo cop dragged into a joint investigation with an FBI agent over a missing politician’s daughter (Lily James), while a former yakuza figure out for revenge works an angle neither sees coming. It’s a setup built for Miike’s tangled plotting and gonzo violence. World premiering at Toronto, screenwriter Daisuke Tengan, of Miike’s “13 Assassins,” returns to script this one. NR



	

					Brace Your Heart
									Credit: Sophia Olsson
	



	“Brace Your Heart” (Amanda Kernell, Nordisk Film Production, Forest People, Compass Films, Invictus, Nordisk Film Production Denmark, Filmpool Nord, SVT, Film i Väst, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Iceland, Bulgaria, Platform)“Sámi Blood” director Amanda Kernell talks about responsibility – and how heavy that burden can be. Her protagonist, Ejva, has been harmed but also has her family, and her Sámi community, to consider. Kernell told Variety: “What can be forgiven? And what if you live in a place where everything has to be, because it can be a matter of survival?” It’s not easy, but there’s a way out of the trauma. Speaking up, however terrifying, might be just what you need to heal. MB
	



	

					Children Untold
									K2 Pictures
	



	“Children Untold,” (Nishikawa Miwa, K2 Pictures, Japan, Platform — Opening Film)Nishikawa Miwa, returning to TIFF for a fourth year, opens this year’s Platform program with a story set in Tokyo during the last days and aftermath of World War II. Orphaned at 12 and born to a pair of musicians, the film’s central girl adopts a boy’s disguise to survive the city’s underworld, while a former teacher, carrying her own guilt, keeps quiet watch over her. Adapted from Nishikawa’s own unpublished novel and starring Ami Koyae, Fumi Nikaido and Koji Yakusho, it’s a Platform opener from one of Japan’s most reliably acclaimed filmmakers, in a section whose winner now has a direct line to the international feature Oscar race. NR



	

					The Daughters of Abraham
									Courtesy of TIFF
	



	“The Daughters of Abraham,” (Hanael El Yousfi, CG Cinéma, France 2 Cinéma, France, Discovery)At the film’s get-go, a Marseilles university lecturer quotes Aristotle’s take on happiness as the freedom to become what one is. Achieving that, however, is no slam dunk, as Arab Myriam and BFF Jewish Eva’s modern assumptions about sex and anti-patriarchy grate against their still traditional worlds. Capturing with flair and ambivalence a sense of community, its events – a Marrakech nightclub, a Marseilles Arab wedding and Jewish dinner – its dynamics and resilient impositions – El Yousfi’s stylish debut is produced by Charles Gillibert, behind many of France’s higher-profile arthouse plays (“The Chronology of Water,” “Minotaur”) and sold by Les Films du Losange. JH    



	

					Djinn Wedding
									Courtesy of TIFF
	



	“Djinn Wedding” (Ferit Karahan, Ferit Karahan Films, Royal Pictures, Maya Films, Arya Yapim, Turkey, Platform)“Can a person who denies their own darkness truly change their fate?” is the question that drove director Ferik Karahan to make his third feature film. A story about family, history and Anatolian folk tales, the film follows four siblings across three periods of time as their dark secrets and traumas begin to unravel during a family wedding. Dealing with the universal themes of  loss, guilt and mourning, this is Karahan’s follow-up feature to “Brother’s Keeper,” which won the Fipresci’s Berlin Panorama Award. RP



	

					Faith
									Courtesy of TIFF
	



	”Faith,” (Paul Andrew Williams, Giant Productions, Homefront Productions, Blazing Griffin, Miria Talent, U.K. Special Presentations)Already a talking point at Toronto after an early screening, with Erin Doherty (“Adolescence,” “The Crown”) gleaning rave reviews for her performance as a single mother charmed by a mysterious but increasingly sinister stranger (James McAvoy), then tortured by grief as horrifying tragedy occurs. Generally, the film has drawn upbeat reaction as well. “Intense performances power startling and unsettling tale of mysterious suitor,” says the Guardian.  A drama with a supernatural build from Paul Andrew Williams (“Bull,” “Dragonfly”), an invigorating presence on the British film scene. JH
	



	

					Le Faux Soir
									Courtesy of Goodfellas
	



	“Le Faux Soir,” (Michaël R. Roskam, Frakas Productions, Rectangle Production, Goodfellas, Harbor Men Pictures, Belgium, France, Special Presentation)Oscar-nominated “Bullhead” helmer Roskam hadn’t directed a feature film in his home country of Belgium since 2017’s “Race and the Jailbird.” His homecoming is a fitting one, a highly ambitious historical thriller set in 1943 and relaying the real-life case of a group of Resistance fighters who printed a fake edition of Belgium’s leading newspaper Le Soir, which had been turned into a propaganda tool during the Nazi occupation. The case is widely considered to be the world’s first media hack, with Roskam’s fast-paced thriller honing in on the past to paint a vivid picture of the present. RSR



	

					Four Seasons in Java
	



	“Four Seasons in Java,” (Kamila Andini, Forka Films, Indonesia, France, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, Centrepiece)Kamila Andini sets her latest against the volcanic backdrop of Mount Bromo, following Putri Marino’s Pertiwi as she returns to her village after years in prison for killing a man who tried to rape her. Old family wounds and a wary community await her, and Andini slides between registers — grounded drama one moment, something closer to myth or speculative fiction the next. Arya Saloka and Christine Hakim round out the cast. Producer Ifa Isfansyah pictured Bromo as the setting nearly a decade before shooting began. It’s Andini’s return to TIFF after winning the Platform Award in 2021 with “Yuni,” and one of this year’s most striking Southeast Asian entries. NR



	

					Future Tense
									Courtesy of TIFF
	



	“Future Tense” (Jenna Cato Bass, Causeway Films, Benchfilms and Fox Fire Film, South Africa,Australia; Centrepiece) Five years after thrilling TIFF audiences with “Good Madam,” a Jordan Peele-esque creeper that explored the real-life horror of post-apartheid trauma, Jenna Cato Bass returns with the sci-fi feature “Future Tense.” Set in a near future on the brink of climate collapse, it unpacks weighty issues like climate change, human guilt and South African identity through the story of a mixed-race couple offered a chance to travel back in time. The film should cement Bass’ status as one of their country’s most inventive and provocative filmmakers. Specialty distributors might want to take note: Shudder swooped on “Good Madam” after its Toronto premiere. CV
	



	

					Glaxo
									Courtesy of RT Features, Rei Pictures
	



	“Glaxo,” (Benjamín Naishtat, RT Features, Rei Pictures, Brazil, Argentina, Special Presentations) “This is the story of betrayal,” says Miguelito, the narrator of “Glaxo.” In fact, he’s only half right. This is the story of seemingly endemic betrayals, braiding narratives in 1956, 1957, and 1984 – the tale of heinous police commissioner Folcada, Miguelito, besotted by his dazzling wife Miranda and his former teen friend “Flaco” Tepermann, just out of jail 25 years later. A return to the multi-genre high-style and collective psychology portrait of “Rojo” marking one of the most awaited Latin American films of the year.



	

					Growth of the Soil
									Courtesy of 4 ½ Fiction
	



	“Growth of the Soil” (Hans Petter Molland, 4 1/2 Fiction, Scanbox Entertainment, Norway, Special Presentation)Molland, known for his collabs with Stellan Skarsgård, takes on the classic novel by Knut Hamsun and ends up with an epic love story spanning decades – the kind not seen since “Doctor Zhivago.” In his film – recently selected as Norway’s Oscar submission – two people come together in order to survive, only to realize they can’t live without each other. But their relationship, just like the wilderness that surrounds them, has to face destruction as well. That’s just the way the world works. MB



	

					Happily Ever After
									Happily Ever After Toronto Film Festival
	



	“Happily Ever After,” (Feng-I Fiona Roan, Splash Pictures, Taiwan, Special Presentations)Feng-I Fiona Roan’s sophomore feature follows two sisters pulling in opposite directions: Kitty, the family favorite, is riding a promotion and an engagement to a wealthy man, while Claire keeps disappointing their parents chasing a life of her own. An abandoned cat that lands in their laps cracks open old wounds. Shuhua of K-pop group i-dle makes her acting debut opposite Xuan Chen, with Kuei-Mei Yang and Jack Kao rounding out the cast. Roan became the Golden Horse Awards’ first female Best New Director winner for her 2021 debut “American Girl,” and this world premiere is one of the fest’s most anticipated follow-ups from a filmmaker on the rise. NR



	

					Idda
									Credit: Simona Pampallona
	



	“Idda” (Irene Dionisio, Kino Produzioni, Rai Cinema, Andromeda Film, EDI, Wise Pictures, Italy, Platform)A TIFF Platform buzz title, praised for its charm and sensuality, this is a portrait of friendship between two childhood friends who decide to climb Mount Etna, an active volcano on the Eastern Coast of Sicily.  Carefree Sofia and the more restrained Adele couldn’t be more different, but they share an unbreakable bond that will be tested when confronted with bottled-up resentment, past secrets and the fear of change as they make their way up the treacherous mountainside.  This is Irene Dionisio’s sophomore feature following her 2016 debut “Le Ultime Cose.” RP
	



	

					On Behalf of My Son
									Courtesy of Filmes de Plástico
	



	“On Behalf of My Son,” (Gabriel Martins, Filmes de Plástico, Netflix Brazil, Platform)When festivals were still finding their footing following the COVID-19 pandemic, Gabriel Martins made waves at Sundance with the tender family drama “Mars One.” Four years later, the Brazilian director returns with a major production that reunites him with Rejane Faria, who plays the mother of a bus driver who apparently killed himself and dozens of passengers in a planned suicide-crash. The film comes onto the festival circuit with the weight of Netflix’s backing and gunning to become Brazil’s Oscar entry, due to be announced mid-September. Following two banner years with “I’m Still Here” and “The Secret Agent,” all eyes are rightly on what Brazil does next. RSR



	

					Onwards and Sideways 
									BBC/Jonathan Birch
	



	“Onwards and Sideways,” (John Madden, John Gore Studios BBC, Hilltop Screen, Kaleidoscope, U.K.)Helmed by Madden, Oscar-nominated for “Shakespeare in Love,” a romantic dramedy starring Oscar nominee Laura Linney and BAFTA winner Rhys Ifans as two people who meet having just received the same Parkinson’s diagnosis with “five good years to live,” their straight talking neurologist (Rory Kinnear) tells them. A bottle half-full, knowing yet upbeat take on the illness written by Paul Mayhew-Archer (“The Vicar of Dibley”) who lives with Parkinson’s. Set for a TIFF gala screening on Sept. 13 and U.K. theatrical release from Icon Film Distribution. CAA Media Finance co-reps North America. JH



	

					Purgatory
									Courtesy of TIFF
	



	“Purgatory,” (Lindsay Lanzillotta, Brave Jayne Films, Canada, U.S., Discovery) Producer Lanzillotta (“The Invitation,” Spin Me Round”) takes her first spin in the director’s chair with ’80s-set coming-of-age dramedy “Purgatory,” assembling a stellar cast to create a family and community dynamic that resonates with emotion and humor. After her mother (Abby Elliott, “The Bear”) moves out to find herself, 13-year-old Beatrice is determined to fix her family, and few other teenage problems, turning to her church’s priest ( J.K. Simmons) for guidance. “Everyone has to realize that their parents are not perfect, that life is not always easy, and that the world is bigger than just themselves,” Lansillotta says. Gersh handles international sales. JP
	



	

									Liam Harkins as Danny in Salvation
	



	“Salvation,“ Tom Nicoll, (Lane Productions with Creative Scotland, U.K., Discovery)Inspired by a self confidence guru, Danny Carter, a dishwasher, becomes a professional life coach. “I can show you how to build a new life and find true happiness,” he promises on social media. Trouble is there’s an elephant in the room: Scottish port Greenock, caught in post-industrial depression and a world dominated by domineering baby boomers such as mentee Scott’s dad who made it in easier times. So the illusions Danny sells are essentially delusions. Finely shot in often hyper character close-ups, a compassionate take on GenZ travails sparking great word of mouth and an auspicious feature debut from Scottish writer-director Tom Nicoll. JH



	

					The Secret Lives of Baba Segi’s Wives
									Courtesy of TIFF
	



	“The Secret Lives of Baba Segi’s Wives” (Daniel Oriahi, EbonyLife Media, Nigeria, Centrepiece)Based on Lola Shoneyin’s 2010 debut novel, “The Secret Lives of Baba Segi’s Wives” is set within a seemingly harmonious polygamous household whose fragile balance is overturned with the arrival of the titular patriarch’s youngest wife. A dramatic comedy that crackles with trademark Nollywood wit, the film marks the return of Nigerian mogul Mo Abudu’s powerhouse production outfit EbonyLife Films to Toronto, the fifth time selected. Oriahi, who helmed the genre-bending Tribeca premiere “The Weekend” in 2024, directs a star-studded cast, back in Toronto after his action comedy “Taxi Driver: Oko Ashewo” — another EbonyLife Films production — bowed at TIFF in 2016. CV



	

					The Smell of Apples
	



	“The Smell of Apples” (John Trengove, Portobello Productions, Cadence, Baldr Film, Quijote Films, South Africa, Netherlands, Chile; Platform)After establishing a foothold in Hollywood with “Manodrome,” his Jesse Eisenberg-starring portrait of toxic masculinity that competed at the 2023 Berlinale, South Africa’s Trengove returns to the native turf he mined to such powerful effect in “The Wound,” his Oscar-shortlisted gay romantic drama. Adapted from Mark Behr’s bestselling, Booker Prize-nominated novel, “The Smell of Apples” is a sensitive portrait of a sheltered 11-year-old white South African boy who gradually comes to realize the horrors of the apartheid system. Produced by Portobello Productions — whose credits include Oscar winners “Kolya” and “Ida” — Cadence, Baldr Film and Quijote Films, the film uses the intimate story of one family to tell a larger tale about the violence lurking behind an idyllic façade. CV
	



	

					Stuffed
									Courtesy of TIFF
	



	“Stuffed,” (Theo Rhys, Agile Films, Fresh Fish Films, BFI, Ffilm Cymru Wales, U.K., Discovery)A taxidermy musical. Finally! But much more, starring Jodie Comer (“Killing Eve”) and opening TIFF’s Discovery program. “Odd and oddly touching,” says Variety. A macabre comedy, love story and musical – song no dance, though Comer does prance in one show-stopping turn as she belts out a song. She plays a wild haired anti-social taxidermist dreaming of stuffing a human specimen, Harry Melling, of “Harry Potter” and “Pillion” fame, is Bernie, an anonymous factory worker who volunteers for embalming. A Gothic but tender, especially when they begin  JH



	

					Sunburn
									Courtesy of TIFF
	



	“Sunburn,” dir. Serville Poblete, Serve, Tinygiant, Canada, CentrepieceAfter scooping a SXSW jury award for his 2026 docu short “In The Morning Sun,” Poblete turns up the heat with “Sunburn,” a hangout film set in St. James Town, the Toronto high-rise community where he grew up­. The story follows three pairs of friends on the cusp of changes they can’t yet see, trying to stay cool and fight the boredom, “kids who look like me, ” he says, “with darker skin, curly hair, raised in immigrant and working-class Toronto.” Sweeping orchestral score by Aaron Paris makes the summer day feel epic, the loose-limbed ensemble performance keeps it grounded. No surprise buyers are circling after the well received first market screening. JP



	

					Talent for Murder
									Courtesy of TIFF
	



	“Talent for Murder,” (Anton Corbijn, LD Entertainment, Brouhaha Entertainment, Lunar Pictures, Lucky Red, U.K., Italy, Gala Presentation)“Hotly anticipated,” Variety reports, starring Helen Mirren as crime writer Patricia Highsmith, the first film for over nine years Corbijn (“Control,”“The American”) with FilmNation Entertainment handling international. The basic plot is known: callow young New York literary agent (Ehrenreich) is dispatched to Switzerland to persuade Highsmith (Mirren) to write one final Ripley thriller. His real motives are, however, rather more Ripley-esque. Co-starring Tony winner Alden Ehrenreich and “House of the Dragon” star Olivia Cooke. Set for an Oct. 23 U.S. debut by Bleecker Street and LD Entertainment. JH  



	

					Toy Gun Bandit
									Courtesy of TIFF
	



	“Toy Gun Bandit,” (dir. Rémi St-Michel, Spécimen Productions, Canada, Centrepiece)For his second feature, Rémi St-Michel explores “what happens when the insatiable need for impressing and belonging gets out of hand.” He does this through the charmingly infuriating character of 15-year-old Felix (non-professional actor Félix Munger) whose life takes an unexpected turn after a prank becomes an actual robbery. The mayhem is further intensified when Félix falls in with an aspiring gangster (David Beaudoin) and a drug addict (Sara Montpetit), the film’s shooting, editing, and sound carrying the frantic energy to the edge. From the producers of “Humanist Vampire Seeking Consenting Suicidal Person,” with h264 distributing in Canada and handling international sales. JP
	



	

					Wild Wild East
									Courtesy Madants
	



	“Wild, Wild East” (Jan Holoubek, Madants, Holograph, Extreme Emotions, Poland, Platform)In his Western-y film, overseen by “The Zone of Interest” producer, Polish director Jan Holoubek takes a page from Tarantino and proves there are different ways to talk about the Second World War. Everyone’s guilty here – mostly of averting their eyes when the unthinkable happens. But it’s not just about poisonous silence, national guilt or the purpose of art when the world is ending; it’s also about many twists and turns, and an ending that throws a straight punch to the head. MB

title: Wisconsin Congressman Tom Tiffany Hospitalized After Plane Makes Emergency Landing in Lake
description:
Wisconsin Rep. Tom Tiffany
                          Hospitalized After Emergency Water Landing M
body:
Wisconsin Rep. Tom Tiffany
                          Hospitalized After Emergency Water Landing Midflight
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 13, 2026
                            6:59 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Wisconsin Congressman and Republican gubernatorial candidate Tom Tiffany is recovering after the small plane he was traveling in was forced to make an emergency landing in Lake Wausau Saturday night.
      
    
            In a statement posted to X, Tiffany explains he was heading home from the La Crosse County Lincoln Day Dinner when the aircraft reportedly lost power while approaching Wausau Downtown Airport. The pilot then put the four-seat plane down on the lake in an emergency water landing.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            The situation quickly turned dangerous after the aircraft began taking on water. Tiffany and the pilot called 911, then got out of the sinking plane and swam toward shallow water, where they waited for rescuers to arrive by boat.
      

            Emergency crews ultimately brought both men to safety and transported them to Aspirus Wausau Hospital. Tiffany said he and the pilot suffered only minor injuries.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Tiffany later expressed gratitude to the pilot and first responders, including the Wausau Fire Department, for getting them out of the water safely. He also said his wife, Chris, was with him at the hospital. The cause of the plane's power loss has not been determined.
      
    
            Tiffany, who represents Wisconsin's 7th Congressional District, is the Republican nominee for governor and is set to face Democratic nominee David Crowley in November.
      
    
            Crowley reacted to the incident by expressing relief that Tiffany and the pilot were not seriously hurt and praising the pilot's actions during the emergency.

title: 'McBee Dynasty' Star Steve McBee Sr. Released From Prison, Shares Heartfelt Reunion Post
description:
Steve McBee Sr.
                          Home After Prison Release ...
                          Reun
body:
Steve McBee Sr.
                          Home After Prison Release ...
                          Reunites With Family
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 13, 2026
                            7:24 AM PDT
                                                                            
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Steve McBee Sr. is back home and back with his family after spending months behind bars ... and the 'McBee Dynasty' patriarch is making it clear he’s appreciating the little things.
      
    
            Steve shared his first public message following his release Saturday, posting a video from his return to the family farm in Gallatin, Missouri. The reality star expressed gratitude for being home and for the blessings in his life.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            His return has been an emotional one for the McBee family. Steve’s son, Steven McBee Jr., celebrated his dad’s release online, while another son, Cole McBee, shared a photo of Steve meeting his newest granddaughter, Tate, who was born while he was incarcerated.
      

            Steve’s freedom comes after he served less than a year of a two-year federal prison sentence. He began his sentence in December 2025 at a federal prison camp in South Dakota after pleading guilty to a federal crop insurance fraud scheme.
      
    
            According to court records, Steve admitted to a scheme involving millions of dollars in crop insurance benefits. He was ultimately ordered to pay more than $4 million in restitution and forfeit more than $3 million to the government.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Steve could have faced a much longer sentence, but the judge ultimately sentenced him to 24 months behind bars, followed by two years of supervised release.
      
    
            His early release was made possible in part by his participation in a program that reduced the amount of time he had to spend in prison. He is expected to spend several months under home confinement.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Steve's legal troubles have been a major storyline on Bravo's "The McBee Dynasty: Real American Cowboys," with cameras documenting the impact his incarceration had on his family and their Missouri farming operation.
      
    
            Before reporting to prison, Steve characterized the experience as something of a “sabbatical” and maintained that he accepted responsibility for his actions.
      
    
            As we previously reported, according to court docs obtained by TMZ, a federal judge denied Steve’s effort to get the civil suit brought by the U.S. government against him tossed out of court -- Steve claimed the government had no case.
      
    
            Now, after months apart, Steve is finally getting what his family has been waiting for ... a chance to be home together again.
